title: Chicken and Leek Pie
subtitle: Creamy chicken and leek filling in a golden puff pastry shell
excerpt: Chicken and leek pie is a gentler, more delicate version of chicken pie: poached chicken in a tarragon cream sauce with softened leeks, enclosed in a full puff pastry shell. The leek and tarragon together give the filling a clean, herbal note. It is well suited to spring and summer as well as colder months.
sourceNotes: The combination of chicken and leek in a pastry crust is a classic of British and Scottish home cooking. Leeks are particularly associated with Welsh and Scottish cooking, where they appear in many traditional savoury dishes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked filling for up to 2 months. Defrost overnight, reheat until hot, then enclose in fresh pastry and bake.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling a day ahead and refrigerate. Assemble and bake on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb with a mild anise flavour, widely used in French and British cooking. French tarragon is the kitchen variety; use it fresh or dried.

content.text: Chicken and leek pie has a lighter, more herbal character than the mushroom version. Poached chicken and sliced leeks go into a

cream sauce, which is then enclosed in a full puff pastry shell. The tarragon lifts the whole dish without dominating. This is a pie you can make with a pan-bought sheet of puff pastry and a good stock, and it looks impressive when it comes out of the oven.

items.prepNote: washed, white and light green parts, sliced
chilled, enough for a base and lid

content.text: Poach {{chicken-breast}} chicken breasts in {{stock-chicken}} of simmering chicken stock for 15 minutes until just cooked through. Lift out and set aside. Strain and keep the stock. When cool, cut the chicken into generous chunks.

In a wide pan, melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter over medium heat. Add {{leek}} sliced leeks and cook gently for 8 minutes until soft and wilted but not coloured. Stir in {{plain-flour}} of flour and cook for 1 minute. Gradually whisk in the warm stock, then {{double-cream}} of double cream. Simmer for 5 minutes until thick and glossy. Stir in the chopped tarragon and {{dijon-mustard}} of Dijon mustard. Season well.
Add the chicken chunks to the sauce. Tip into the pie dish and leave to cool to room temperature.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. If making a full double-crust pie, line the base of the dish with one layer of pastry, prick the base lightly, and bake blind for 10 minutes. For a lid-only version, simply brush the rim and lay the pastry over the cooled filling. Either way, seal the edges, cut a vent, and brush all over with beaten egg.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is risen, puffed, and deep golden. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.

items.symptom: The leeks are watery in the finished pie
items.cause: Leeks release a lot of liquid; they need thorough cooking before the flour is added.
items.fix: Cook the leeks until completely soft and any released liquid has evaporated before adding the flour. This takes 8 to 10 minutes, not less.

items.symptom: The tarragon flavour is too faint
items.cause: Dried tarragon was used, or the fresh herb was added too early and lost its character.
items.fix: Use fresh tarragon and add it at the end, after the sauce is off the heat. Dried tarragon is not a reliable substitute here.

items.symptom: The pastry slides off during baking
items.cause: The filling was too warm or the rim not brushed with egg.
items.fix: Always cool the filling before adding the pastry. Press the egg-brushed rim down firmly before baking.

items.symptom: The chicken is dry in the pie
items.fix: Poach just until the centre is no longer pink, not until fully firm. The chicken heats further inside the pie.

content.text: Chicken and leek is one of the classic pairings of British and Welsh cooking. Leeks are the Welsh national vegetable and appear in traditional broths and pies that predate the chicken-and-mushroom pub standard. This version with tarragon tips toward a slightly French influence, the result of the long culinary exchange across the Channel that shaped British cooking from the eighteenth century onward.
